The rosetta Comparison Set and the bc2sa Bridge Ecosystem

This page introduces two real channels for “leveraging the Rust ecosystem”: the rosetta comparison set — one Rust reference implementation paired with one SLA implementation per topic, used to manually check semantic equivalence; bc2sa — reverse-translating LLVM bitcode into SA, so that Rust/C/C++ compilation outputs enter the SA pipeline directly. After reading it you will be able to judge: which path the Rust code at hand should take, and how much each can currently handle.

Structure and Naming Pattern of the rosetta Tree

demos/rosetta/ currently has 315 consecutively numbered directories (01–315). The root README describes itself as “300 Rust/SLA comparison demos, originating from sci/demos/rosetta”; the actual directory numbering goes up to 315, and from 301 onward they are SLA frontend feature demos (@overload operators, the _ discard slot, using static extensions, async suspension/resumption, etc.). Each directory always contains:

FileContent
main.rsRust reference implementation (kept in its original style)
main.slaCorresponding SLA implementation, most with an @test "rosetta NNN …" self-check block
README.mdOne-sentence description (only 314_async_await_pending_resume and 315_async_thread_pool are missing one for now)
main.sa / cache directoriesSome directories keep compiled SA text and artifacts such as .sla-cache

Semantic Equivalence Labels: The ✅ / ❌ Registration Framing in demo.md

The root demo.md registers, item by item, the semantic matching relationship between “Rust source ↔ SLA file”: ✅ means a direct 1:1 mapping; ❌ means an accepted alternative implementation, subset, or non-1:1 correspondence. There are currently 204 registered lines in total, of which 114 are ✅ and 90 are ❌ (this is a count of the current file contents in the repository; it changes as the code evolves, so do not cite it as a fixed ratio). The reasons on the ❌ lines are written very concretely, for example:

  • 02_mutability: Rust performs a sequence of a shared borrow followed by a mutable borrow on the same variable; SLA can only preserve the final value through a separate immutable helper computation.
  • 04_loop: Rust uses &mut [u8; 4] plus an indexed for loop to rewrite the original buffer; SLA currently consumes the array and substitutes fill(0).
  • 23_nested_loops: Rust uses nested range for; SLA rewrites it as while; the control-flow shape differs but the total is the same.
  • 40_impl_block_state: Rust modifies state in place through &mut self; SLA consumes self and returns a new value, so the semantics are not 1:1.
  • 190_base64_encode_simd: the current SLA source fails locally on the u8 arithmetic chain and never reaches the string collection step.
  • 310–313: the _ discard slot, using static extensions, @overload, and type alias flattening are explicitly registered as “local frontend surface demos, not claims of Rust equivalence”.
WarningThe rosetta tree is positioned as a workbench for manually checking semantic equivalence, not a regression test set. The official documentation explicitly notes that not everything in it runs end to end — for example, 09_async_await is marked in demo.md as “the current SLA version fails on the local checked path; it is not a stable direct correspondence”. Please verify each demo individually before use, and do not assume the whole tree is ready.

Three Typical Comparison Groups

Fully 1:1 case (27_move_semantics, identical line by line except for the entry signature and the self-check block):

// main.rs                          // main.sla
struct Data {                       struct Data {
    value: i32,                         value: i32,
}                                   }

fn consume(data: Data) -> i32 {     fn consume(data: Data) -> i32 {
    data.value                          data.value
}                                   }

Case where a method must be rewritten (59_method_counter): Rust uses &mut self to increment in place, while SLA uses Cell to carry interior mutability, and the method signature is &self:

// Rust                              // Sla
impl Counter {                        impl Counter {
    fn inc(&mut self) {                   fn inc(&self) -> void {
        self.0 += 1;                          let current = self.value.get();
    }                                         self.value.set(current + 1);
}                                             }
                                      }
// 字段声明：struct Counter(i32);  →   struct Counter { value: Cell<i32>, }

Case where Drop must be expanded by hand (101_custom_drop): Rust writes impl Drop so a guard accumulates a count when it goes out of scope; SLA does not support Drop, and rewrites the release order as two explicit accumulations:

// Rust（节选）                        // Sla（节选）
impl Drop for Guard<'_> {             // 无 Drop：按作用域顺序显式累加
    fn drop(&mut self) {              tally = tally + inner_value;
        self.tally.set(               tally = tally + outer_value;
            self.tally.get()          return tally + result;
            + self.value);
    }
}

How to Use This Tree

# 运行目录：sa_plugin_sla 仓库根目录
SA_PLUGIN_DEV=1 sa sla check demos/rosetta/01_hello_world/main.sla
SA_PLUGIN_DEV=1 sa sla build demos/rosetta/01_hello_world/main.sla --out /tmp/01_hello_world.sa
SA_PLUGIN_DEV=1 sa sla test  demos/rosetta/01_hello_world/main.sla

bc2sa: The LLVM Bitcode → SA Bridge

bc2sa is the other path: it does not translate source code, but reverse-translates LLVM bitcode produced by rustc/clang and others into SA text. In theory, any language that can produce LLVM bitcode (Rust, C/C++, Swift, Zig, etc.) can be connected to the SA pipeline through it. Based on bc2sa_evaluation_cn.md (assessment date 2026-06-15, plugin 0.1.0 mainline):

CategoryInstructionStatus
Minimal subset named in the design documentdefine / declare function headersImplemented
alloca / load / storeImplemented
add / sub / mul / comparisons / br / ret / callImplemented
getelementptr byte offsets with fixed boundsImplemented (including out-of-bounds rejection)
Implemented beyond the subsetsdiv/udiv/srem/urem, and/or/xor/shl/lshr/ashr, the full icmp seriesImplemented
trunc/zext/sext/bitcast, string constant globalsImplemented
.ll text input (not only .bc)Implemented
Key gapsphiNot implemented — optimization at -O1 and above necessarily produces it, and rustc's default opt-level=2 also necessarily produces it
switch / selectNot implemented — Rust match expansions and C ternary expressions are often compiled to these two instructions
fadd/fsub/fmul/fdiv/fcmp floating pointNot implemented
extractvalue/insertvalue aggregates, atomic instructionsNot implemented
invoke/landingpad (C++ exceptions)Intentionally not done (conflicts with SA's explicit error model)
NoteThe static safety guardrails are real: if a getelementptr can be proven to cross a fixed array boundary, it directly returns StaticMemoryOverflow, and the CLI exits with the structured error SA-CLI-019; the permission model only allows reading the project directory and spawning /usr/bin/llvm-dis-14, with the argument whitelist -o - <input>. The assessment also makes clear: this strategy only covers statically resolvable constant offsets and does not promise a complete C memory safety proof.

Coverage and Roadmap (with Date Framing)

MetricValueSource and date framing
Share of real code currently translatableO0 baseline + integer operations + static bounds checking ≈ 30%rust_vs_sla_final_cn.md §3.3 / Appendix B (v0.2, 2026-06-15), citing bc2sa_evaluation §1
Generalized completion estimate (by the “can translate a typical Rust/C function” standard)About 25–35%bc2sa_evaluation_cn.md §2.2 (2026-06-15); end-to-end test coverage <5%
Expected after the five P0 items are completeAdd phi / switch / select / floating point / call ownership prefix inference → coverage 70–80%70–80% from rust_vs_sla_final_cn.md §3.3; the P0 list and the “2–3 months” cadence from bc2sa_evaluation_cn.md §4.1 / §6
Long-term visionA complete LLVM bitcode subset; in theory it can consume the entire Rust/C++ ecosystemrust_vs_sla_final_cn.md §3.3

There is therefore one hard constraint on realistic use: bitcode submitted to bc2sa must be forced to O0 (on the Rust side, something like --emit=llvm-bc -Copt-level=0, or preprocess with opt --reg2mem first to remove phi), otherwise you will most likely hit an unsupported instruction. The assessment report also recommends labeling bc2sa as experimental / subset only in external publicity.

A Third Tool: simple_rust_converter (Design Proposal)

What sci/docs/simple_rust_converter.md records is a design proposal, not a delivered tool: bypassing LLVM, it is a source-to-source direct translator (DMT) aimed at the SA-ASM “instruction-level subset”. The core mappings are almost 1:1:

fn name(a: i64) -> i64 { ... }   →  @name(a: i64) -> i64:   （自动插入 L_ENTRY 标签）
let x = a + b;                   →  x = add a, b
if cond { A } else { B }         →  br cond -> L_TRUE, L_FALSE（生成标签并跳转）
drop(x);                         →  !x
return val;                      →  return val

The idea is to reuse the lowering logic already in the SAX parser (with a proposed new src/sax/rust_flavor.zig), scan linearly and flatten brace blocks into an SA-ASM label flow, with variable names mapped directly to an unlimited number of virtual registers; the document also suggests compiling it into WASM as the “Simple Rust to SA” button for Monaco Editor in the Playground. Its positioning is clear: sacrifice ecosystem compatibility in exchange for an extremely fast response, suitable for demonstrating SA's core ownership concepts, not suitable for real engineering migration.
